card.title: SEAHAWK
card.flavorText: The Curtiss SC Seahawk was a single-seat scout seaplane developed for the US Navy during WWII. The first prototype flew on 16 February 1944 in Columbus Ohio and production orders followed even before flight tests finished. It was designed to replace earlier types such as the Curtiss SO3C Seamew and the Vought OS2U Kingfisher and was regarded as likely America's best scout floatplane by the end of the war. A total of around 577 SC-1 aircraft were built, entering service in October 1944 aboard ships such as USS Guam. The Seahawk carried two Browning M2 12.7 mm machine guns in the wings and two small underwing racks capable of carrying radar gear or light bombs. A bunk in the rear fuselage allowed rescue or personnel transfer. Its main float design proved problematic for bomb storage so was later modified to carry extra fuel. The Seahawk first saw combat in June 1945 during operations around Borneo, though its late arrival meant limited wartime use. It continued flying postwar until around 1949, when helicopters replaced floatplanes for scouting on battleships and cruisers.

historyPhotoDescription.SourceString: A Seahawk being recovered by the cruiser USS Alaska during the Battle of Iwo Jima in 1945. The aircraft awaits pickup by the ship’s crane after taxiing onto a landing mat.
